### Biographical Overview
- **Full Name**: Erik Ninn-Hansen
- **Born**: October 17, 1922, in Copenhagen, Denmark
- **Died**: May 21, 2014 (aged 91), in Copenhagen
- **Nationality**: Danish
- **Education**: Earned a law degree (cand.jur.) from the University of Copenhagen in 1949
- **Early Life**: During World War II, he was active in the Danish resistance movement, notably in the group *Holger Danske*, opposing the German occupation.

### Political Career
- **Party Affiliation**: Conservative People's Party (*Det Konservative Folkeparti*)
- **Parliament**: Member of the Folketing (Danish Parliament) for the Copenhagen constituency from 1964 to 1990.
- **Party Leadership**: Chairman of the Conservative People's Party from 1974 to 1977.
- **Ministerial Roles**: 
  - Minister of Justice and Minister for Ecclesiastical Affairs in the Schlüter I, II, and III cabinets (September 10, 1982 – January 25, 1989) under Prime Minister Poul Schlüter.
  - Known for a hardline stance on law and order, immigration, and integration policies.
- **Other Roles**: Prior to national politics, he worked as a lawyer in private practice and was involved in Copenhagen municipal politics.

This scandal defined his legacy and had profound implications for Danish constitutional law and politics.

- **Background**: In the mid-1980s, Denmark received a significant influx of Tamil refugees fleeing the Sri Lankan Civil War. Concerned about rising numbers, Ninn-Hansen sought to limit family reunifications without publicly changing asylum policy.
- **Actions**: In late 1987, he secretly instructed the Danish Immigration Service to halt processing of family reunification applications from Tamils submitted after November 1, 1987. - **Exposure**: The scheme unraveled in 1988–1989 through media reports and parliamentary inquiries. Critics argued it was discriminatory, unlawful, and undermined the rule of law.
- **Parliamentary Inquiry**: A commission of inquiry (the "Tamil Commission") was established in 1989. Its 1991 report concluded that Ninn-Hansen had acted unlawfully and that Prime Minister Schlüter had failed to adequately inform parliament, contributing to Schlüter's resignation in 1993.
- **Resignation**: Ninn-Hansen resigned as Minister of Justice on January 25, 1989.

  - Initially acquitted by the Eastern High Court (*Østre Landsret*) in 1993.

  - First conviction of a Danish minister for crimes committed while in office.
  - Reinforced constitutional principles of ministerial accountability and transparency.
  - Sparked national debates on immigration policy, racism, and the balance between administrative discretion and legal boundaries.
  - Led to reforms in how ministries document decisions and interact with agencies.

### Later Life and Legacy
- **Post-Scandal**: After resignation, he largely withdrew from public life. In his 1997 memoir *Fra min tid* ("From My Time"), he defended his actions as necessary for Denmark's interests and maintained he acted in good faith.
- **Personal Life**: Married to Inger Ninn-Hansen (1925–2009), who was also a Conservative Folketing member (1971–1994). They had children. His wife was not formally implicated in the scandal.
- **Death**: Died peacefully in Copenhagen in 2014. Obituaries acknowledged his early resistance work and political contributions but emphasized the Tamil Case as his defining legacy.

  - Viewed critically in legal and political scholarship as a cautionary tale about abuse of power. 
  - The case remains a staple in Danish law and political science curricula.
  - Some conservative commentators have revisited his stance sympathetically in later immigration debates, though the conviction stands as a legal landmark.
- **Honors**: Previously awarded the Order of the Dannebrog (Knight, 1971; later Commander); no public record indicates revocation post-conviction.

- **Resistance Legacy**: His WWII resistance activities were widely respected and often cited in early biographies.
- **Cultural Impact**: The Tamil Case has been referenced in Danish media, documentaries, and academic works on governance. It is sometimes compared to other ministerial scandals globally for its implications on executive accountability.

- **Born**: October 17, 1922, in Copenhagen, Denmark
- **Died**: May 21, 2014 (aged 91), in Copenhagen
- **Nationality**: Danish
- **Education**: Earned a law degree (cand.jur.) from the University of Copenhagen in 1949
- **Early Life**: During World War II, he was active in the Danish resistance movement, notably in the group *Holger Danske*, opposing the German occupation.

### Political Career
- **Party Affiliation**: Conservative People's Party (*Det Konservative Folkeparti*)
- **Parliament**: Member of the Folketing (Danish Parliament) for the Copenhagen constituency from 1964 to 1990.
- **Party Leadership**: Chairman of the Conservative People's Party from 1974 to 1977.
- **Ministerial Roles**: 
  - Minister of Justice and Minister for Ecclesiastical Affairs in the Schlüter I, II, and III cabinets (September 10, 1982 – January 25, 1989) under Prime Minister Poul Schlüter.
  - Known for a hardline stance on law and order, immigration, and integration policies.
- **Other Roles**: Prior to national politics, he worked as a lawyer in private practice and was involved in Copenhagen municipal politics.

### The Tamil Case (Tamil-sagen)
This scandal defined his legacy and had profound implications for Danish constitutional law and politics.

- **Background**: In the mid-1980s, Denmark received a significant influx of Tamil refugees fleeing the Sri Lankan Civil War. Concerned about rising numbers, Ninn-Hansen sought to limit family reunifications without publicly changing asylum policy.
- **Actions**: In late 1987, he secretly instructed the Danish Immigration Service to halt processing of family reunification applications from Tamils submitted after November 1, 1987. The instruction was given orally, bypassing formal channels and legal procedures, with the aim of artificially suppressing approval numbers.
- **Exposure**: The scheme unraveled in 1988–1989 through media reports and parliamentary inquiries. Critics argued it was discriminatory, unlawful, and undermined the rule of law.
- **Parliamentary Inquiry**: A commission of inquiry (the "Tamil Commission") was established in 1989. Its 1991 report concluded that Ninn-Hansen had acted unlawfully and that Prime Minister Schlüter had failed to adequately inform parliament, contributing to Schlüter's resignation in 1993.
- **Resignation**: Ninn-Hansen resigned as Minister of Justice on January 25, 1989.
- **Criminal Proceedings**:
  - Initially acquitted by the Eastern High Court (*Østre Landsret*) in 1993.
  - The prosecution appealed; in 1995, Denmark's Supreme Court (*Højesteret*) convicted him of *misbrug af embedsmæssig myndighed* (abuse of official authority).
  - **Sentence**: 120 days' imprisonment, suspended, plus court costs. The verdict emphasized that ministers are criminally liable for deliberate misuse of power.
- **Significance**: 
  - First conviction of a Danish minister for crimes committed while in office.
  - Reinforced constitutional principles of ministerial accountability and transparency.
  - Sparked national debates on immigration policy, racism, and the balance between administrative discretion and legal boundaries.
  - Led to reforms in how ministries document decisions and interact with agencies.

### Later Life and Legacy
- **Post-Scandal**: After resignation, he largely withdrew from public life. In his 1997 memoir *Fra min tid* ("From My Time"), he defended his actions as necessary for Denmark's interests and maintained he acted in good faith.
- **Personal Life**: Married to Inger Ninn-Hansen (1925–2009), who was also a Conservative Folketing member (1971–1994). They had children. His wife was not formally implicated in the scandal.
- **Death**: Died peacefully in Copenhagen in 2014. Obituaries acknowledged his early resistance work and political contributions but emphasized the Tamil Case as his defining legacy.
- **Historical Assessment**: 
  - Viewed critically in legal and political scholarship as a cautionary tale about abuse of power. 
  - The case remains a staple in Danish law and political science curricula.
  - Some conservative commentators have revisited his stance sympathetically in later immigration debates, though the conviction stands as a legal landmark.
- **Honors**: Previously awarded the Order of the Dannebrog (Knight, 1971; later Commander); no public record indicates revocation post-conviction.

### Additional Notes
- **Resistance Legacy**: His WWII resistance activities were widely respected and often cited in early biographies.
- **Cultural Impact**: The Tamil Case has been referenced in Danish media, documentaries, and academic works on governance. It is sometimes compared to other ministerial scandals globally for its implications on executive accountability.
- **Common Misconceptions**: 
  - The case was not about denying asylum outright but about procedural manipulation to limit family reunifications. 
  - While discriminatory intent was alleged by critics, the conviction centered on *abuse of procedure*, not racism per se. 
  - Prime Minister Schlüter's resignation (1993) was directly tied to the cover-up aspects of this scandal, though Schlüter himself faced no criminal charges.
